review_title: impact of GEnAI on OSS Projects review
review_template_title: impact of GEnAI on OSS Projects review
paper_title: Developers and Generative AI: A Study of Self-Admitted Usage in Open Source Projects
logical_feed_name: impact of GEnAI on OSS Projects

values.study_identification: Mining-based replication and extension study that classifies self-admitted uses of ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot in OSS commits, issues, and PRs, deriving task taxonomies and comparing with prior findings.
values.study_objective: To identify and categorize software-development tasks for which developers self-admit using ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot in OSS projects, assess perceived usefulness, and compare changes since a prior ChatGPT-only study.
study_population: Open-source GitHub repositories (>=10 stars) with commits, PRs, or issues mentioning ChatGPT or Copilot
Manually validated instances: 343 ChatGPT and 281 Copilot across 492 projects
Automatically classified Copilot instances (e.g., PR/commit descriptions, Autofix patterns)
values.study_period: GitHub mining performed January 29, 2025; compared to prior dataset collected in early June 2023.
values.genai_definition: Generative AI operationalized as Large Language Model-based assistants: ChatGPT (web/chat) and GitHub Copilot (IDE-integrated, with features such as PR description generation and Autofix).
authors_limitations: Observes only self-admitted or tool-attributed uses; silent or undisclosed uses are not captured.
Focuses on textual content of commits, PRs, and issues; excludes other locations (e.g., code comments, discussions).
Manual labeling subject to subjectivity; mitigated via dual coding and conflict resolution.
Exact LLM versions, prompts, and settings are unknown; context windows and tool configurations may vary.
Limited to ChatGPT and Copilot and to GitHub-hosted OSS projects.
High false-positive rate for some Copilot issue mentions; many Copilot cases auto-classified via templates/patterns.
rq_1: Patterns show widespread Copilot use for process automation (e.g., PR/commit descriptions) and ChatGPT use across software quality, documentation, and learning, with differing success rates and roles.
ChatGPT is frequently used for debugging and fixing; success is mixed (~50% for fixing), while learning/how-to uses often fail (73% incorrect).
Documentation generation is common and largely successful (ChatGPT ~90% success; Copilot also widely used).
Feature implementation/enhancement is commonly self-admitted (ChatGPT 84 artifacts; ~80% success; Copilot 51).
Development-environment tasks (e.g., CI integration, Actions, Docker) are admitted for ChatGPT with ~60% success; Copilot is tightly integrated with GitHub workflows.
Copilot supports refactoring and testing more frequently than ChatGPT, reflecting benefits of IDE integration and repository context.
rq1_verification_accountability: Human review and discussion in PRs/issues often assess AI-generated changes or descriptions.
Some projects integrate ChatGPT-based reviews into CI to provide preliminary automated feedback.
Copilot Autofix integrates with GitHub code scanning; suggestions appear as attributed fixes for human acceptance.
rq1_project_characteristics: Repositories hosted on GitHub with at least 10 stars.
Projects employing CI/CD workflows where ChatGPT-based reviewing or Actions/Docker changes were attempted.
rq1_project_type: Varied OSS software projects across languages and domains on GitHub.
rq1_project_size_age: Not systematically characterized; projects had >=10 stars; examples include small to medium repositories.
rq1_technical_context: Use of GitHub PRs, issues, commits; CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions; Docker; IDE integration via Copilot.
rq1_outcome_construct: Increased availability of structured PR/commit/issue descriptions via Copilot integration
Software quality support (debugging, fixing, refactoring, testing) with mixed effectiveness
Learning support often unreliable due to hallucinations
Automation of development-environment tasks (CI/Actions/Docker) with moderate success
rq1_outcome_measure: Copilot auto-attribution: 1,212 commits and 28,004 PRs with generated descriptions; 633 commits and 507 PRs labeled ‘copilot autofix’ (Table 2).
ChatGPT software quality category: 100 artifacts; fixing increased vs prior study; ~50% of fixing cases successful (Section 3.1.6).
ChatGPT documentation: 46 instances; ~90% successful (Section 3.1.7). Copilot documentation: 44 commits + 1 issue + 12 PRs (Fig. 2/3).
Learning/how-to uses incorrect in 73% of artifacts (Section 3.1.3).
Development environment: 24 ChatGPT artifacts; ~60% successful; includes CI review integration and Actions/Docker updates (Section 3.1.5).
Translation/migration across languages via ChatGPT observed (e.g., 8 instances; Fig. 1/Fig. 3).
rq1_beneficiary: Maintainers and reviewers (better summaries, preliminary reviews)
Individuals/newcomers (learning attempts), though often harmed by hallucinations
rq1_cost_bearer: Reviewers/maintainers (need to verify AI outputs, ownership concerns)
rq1_time_horizon: Short term, observable in current PRs/commits; comparison with prior (June 2023) indicates evolving patterns by Jan 2025.
rq1_associations: Copilot’s IDE/GitHub integration correlates with higher prevalence in process automation, refactoring, and testing than ChatGPT.
General-purpose ChatGPT more prevalent in debugging, documentation, brainstorming/learning but with hallucination risks.
rq1_association_pattern: Higher use for PR/commit description generation, refactoring, testing with Copilot
Higher use for debugging discussions, learning queries, documentation with ChatGPT
rq1_association_evidence: Table 2 automatic counts for Copilot; taxonomy counts in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3.
Section 3.1 vs 3.2 comparative narrative and category frequencies.
rq1_boundary_condition: Self-admission bias limits observation to disclosed or auto-attributed uses (Section 1 and Threats).
Task success varies by need for up-to-date knowledge and availability of IDE context.
rq1_supporting_extract: Table 2: Copilot process → creating commit/issue/pr description: 1,212 commits and 28,004 PRs; software quality → fixing: 633 commits, 507 PRs.
Section 3.1.6: “∼50% of the instances assigned to the software quality → fixing sub-category have been labeled as ‘successful’.”
Section 3.1.3: “In 73% of artifacts … the support provided by ChatGPT was incorrect.”
Section 3.1.7: “… we mostly found successful applications of ChatGPT for generating documentation (∼90%).”
Section 3.1.5: “… we marked as successful ∼60% of the instances in the development environment category.”
Fig. 3: Documentation counts (ChatGPT 46; Copilot 57); Refactoring (ChatGPT 9; Copilot 24); Testing (ChatGPT 8; Copilot 22); Translation category present for ChatGPT.
rq_2: IDE-integrated Copilot reduces context switching and leverages repository context and GitHub workflows, fostering automation of PR/commit descriptions and support for refactoring/testing; outcome is improved availability of project metadata and technical changes subject to human review.

Using ChatGPT for learning/how-to on libraries/tools can produce hallucinated guidance; outcome is incorrect configurations or ineffective attempts, potentially harming technical quality and individual learning.
Self-admitted traces and tool attributions create provenance for AI-assisted artifacts; potential governance outcome is increased transparency for trust/licensing, though not empirically evaluated.
rq2_mechanism: Copilot IDE/GitHub integration → fewer context switches and direct access to code changes/metadata → increased automation of PR/commit descriptions and in-IDE assistance for refactoring/testing.
ChatGPT used for ‘how to use a library/framework/tool’ → hallucinated or outdated instructions → failed integrations and negative reports in issues; harms learning and can degrade technical quality.
Self-disclosure/tool attribution in commits/issues/PRs → visible provenance of AI involvement → supports transparency/trust/licensing assessment.
rq2_antecedent: Adoption of Copilot within IDE and GitHub (PR templates, code scanning Autofix).
Developers querying ChatGPT for technology usage and integration guidance.
Developers including AI-use notes; Copilot/Autofix leaving attribution strings.
rq2_intermediate_process: Reduced context switching; automatic summarization; suggestions within coding context.
Hallucinations/misinformation steer users toward incorrect steps; issues opened after failed attempts.
Presence of explicit attributions or self-reports links artifacts to AI assistance.
rq2_mechanism_outcome: Greater availability of structured PR/commit descriptions and in-IDE assistance for code changes (subject to human review).
Incorrect configurations and ineffective fixes; increased rework; negative user experiences in issues.
Improved traceability/provenance for AI-generated artifacts; potential support for governance and trust.
rq2_boundary_condition: Effects depend on task type and need for repository context; IDE integration favors process/refactoring/testing tasks.
Learning outcomes depend on freshness of knowledge and specificity; hallucinations prevalent in how-to queries.
Only observed where developers disclose or tools auto-attribute; silent cases remain unseen.
rq2_governance_decision: anecdotal examples for pro and anti
rq2_decision_actor: commiters and contributor, but anecdotal examples
rq2_supporting_extract: Table 2 and Section 3.2.3: large numbers of Copilot-generated PR/commit descriptions; Section 3.2.4: higher prevalence of refactoring/testing with Copilot.
Section 3.1.3: “In 73% of artifacts … the support provided by ChatGPT was incorrect.”
Throughout and Section 2.2: reliance on self-disclosure and tool-generated templates/patterns (e.g., “generated by Copilot”, “copilot autofix”).
